title: Reviews, the Capitol session and Barry Ulanov
summary: A badly set-up 1950 Capitol date was panned by Ulanov, who later reversed himself after hearing Hug live; commercial pressure on bands.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Okay. Now, I haven't been on the jazz scene very long, but ever since I've been on and I've been reading in jazz journals, it seems to me that you've, I've never seen a review that says anything bad about Alman Haugen. I've read the old jazz record magazine and Record Changer and Downbeat and Metronome. I really don't think that you ever had a negative review. It's a remarkable thing. Do you collect your clippings? Do you save these things? Yes.

I have tried to save most of them, Charlie, and some of them are very, very flattering and as you say, I've gotten some mighty good reviews. I think about the worst review that I ever received when you're talking about receiving bad ones was back in 1950. I cut some sides for Capital, Capital Recording Company was down there and they got a very bad setup to do it. They put up, they wanted to get an old honky-tonk style of piano and they had nothing to do with but to put an old chain across the keys, across the strings, you know, and the sound came out very cluttered up and very corny-like and Barry Ulenoff who was reviewing records in the metronome at that time, you know, he was really a tough critic, you know, and he got a hold of these recordings that I made and boy, did he pan them.
I remember correctly, I think that the A&R job was sort of leaning towards a commercial on that session too, wasn't it?

It was, yes, they wanted strictly commercial and we leaned more a little bit towards corny ragtime, you know, and of course Barry Ulenoff got this and this was supposed to be representative of true New Orleans Dixieland, you know, and he says, well, if this is what it is, he says, I don't want it, you see, so many people began writing him in and telling him that he was very wrong about his opinion of me as a pianist, that when he came to New Orleans, he made it a point to come to the Bayou Bar at the Pontchartrain Hotel and I recognized him by his pictures, you know, so I didn't say anything and I started turning on some progressive music for him, you know, some of the big spider back and some of the progressive music that I knew and I could see his face beaming, you know, when I got up, when I went over there, he called me, when I got up, he called me over, he says, I'm Barry Ulenoff, I said, yes, I knew, he said, you sound a lot different than you did on those records, see, so when he went back, he gave me a review again and he called me the greatest Dixieland pianist that he had heard in modern times and said that I was not only a great Dixieland pianist but a great modern pianist, so I thought that was quite flattering.

It seems like major labels so often take our bands and they dress them up and then they lose all the flavor, all the natural feeling that the groups and individuals actually project into their playing in the normal conditions. Remember when they got Hoda Sharky and made him do Pizza Pie Boogie and some other, Mickey Mouse, that's right, where the band was really great, you remember that band around 49, you were talking about, it was really wonderful and Capital lost the band when they tried to record commercials.

That's right, they started trying to make him record commercial but it just wasn't a real good commercial. This is a good point, Charlie, I think that when you do commercial, you have to really do it real good or either just let it alone.
